claim: Protection against malaria in humans can be achieved by repeated exposure to infected mosquito bites during prophylactic chloroquine treatment (chemoprophylaxis and sporozoites (CPS)).
source: Protection against malaria in humans can be achieved by repeated exposure to infected mosquito bites during prophylactic chloroquine treatment (chemoprophylaxis and sporozoites (CPS)).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established research on CPS immunization in humans.

claim: Immunization with Plasmodium chabaudi by mosquito bite under chloroquine cover does not generate pre-erythrocytic immunity.
source: Immunization with Plasmodium chabaudi by mosquito bite under chloroquine cover does not generate pre-erythrocytic immunity, which is acquired only after immunization with high sporozoite doses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing no difference in liver parasite burden between CPS immunized and control mice.

claim: Pre-erythrocytic immunity is acquired only after immunization with high sporozoite doses.
source: Immunization with Plasmodium chabaudi by mosquito bite under chloroquine cover does not generate pre-erythrocytic immunity, which is acquired only after immunization with high sporozoite doses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced liver parasite burden after immunization with 10,000 sporozoites.

claim: CPS immunization by bite elicits long-lived protection against blood-stage parasites.
source: Instead, CPS immunization by bite elicits long-lived protection against blood-stage parasites.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced blood-stage parasitemia 100 days after immunization.

claim: Blood-stage immunity is effective against a virulent, genetically distinct strain of P. chabaudi.
source: Blood-stage immunity is effective against a virulent, genetically distinct strain of P. chabaudi.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing protection against heterologous P. chabaudi CB challenge.

claim: If exposure to blood-stage parasitemia is extended, blood-stage parasites induce cross-stage immunity targeting pre-erythrocytic stages.
source: Importantly, if exposure to blood-stage parasitemia is extended, blood-stage parasites induce cross-stage immunity targeting pre-erythrocytic stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced liver parasite burden after extended blood-stage infection.

claim: Vaccines are usually successful if they mimic naturally acquired immune responses.
source: Vaccines are usually successful if they mimic these naturally acquired immune responses (Fox, 1984; Mielcarek et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on vaccine development.

claim: There is no licensed vaccine for human parasitic diseases like malaria.
source: While protection against viruses and bacteria can be induced by vaccination with killed (inactivated) or live-attenuated pathogens (Delany et al., 2014), there is no licensed vaccine for human parasitic diseases like malaria that pose a major global health burden.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about the state of malaria vaccine development at the time of publication.

claim: The apicomplexan malaria parasite Plasmodium is transmitted by bites of female anopheline mosquitoes.
source: The apicomplexan malaria parasite Plasmodium is transmitted by bites of female anopheline mosquitoes.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about malaria transmission.

claim: Sporozoites injected into the dermis migrate to the liver, where they establish a clinically silent infection of hepatocytes.
source: In the vertebrate host, sporozoites injected into the dermis migrate to the liver, where they establish a clinically silent infection of hepatocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of the Plasmodium life cycle.

claim: Merozoites are released from the liver and invade erythrocytes, leading to an exponential asexual replication cycle.
source: Merozoites are then released from the liver and invade erythrocytes, leading to an exponential asexual replication cycle that is entirely responsible for the clinical signs and symptoms associated with malaria.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of the Plasmodium life cycle.

claim: The asexual replication cycle in erythrocytes is entirely responsible for the clinical signs and symptoms associated with malaria.
source: Merozoites are then released from the liver and invade erythrocytes, leading to an exponential asexual replication cycle that is entirely responsible for the clinical signs and symptoms associated with malaria.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of malaria pathogenesis.

claim: Immunity against severe disease can be acquired following repeated infection, but sterile parasite clearance is rarely achieved.
source: Immunity against severe disease can be acquired following repeated infection, but sterile parasite clearance is rarely achieved (Goncalves et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on naturally acquired immunity to malaria.

claim: Clinically immune adults in endemic areas still harbor parasites in their blood-stream.
source: Clinically immune adults in endemic areas still harbor parasites in their blood-stream (Okell et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on asymptomatic malaria carriage.

claim: Asymptomatic carriers develop gametocytes, the form transmissible to mosquitoes.
source: These asymptomatic carriers also develop gametocytes, the form transmissible to mosquitoes, thereby allowing the parasite to complete its life cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of the Plasmodium life cycle and transmission.

claim: To achieve malaria control and eventually eradication, transmission must be blocked.
source: To achieve malaria control and eventually eradication, transmission must be blocked (Kappe et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on malaria control strategies.

claim: A vaccine that protects against pre-erythrocytic parasites would greatly facilitate malaria control and eradication.
source: A vaccine that protects against pre-erythrocytic parasites, and thus outperforms naturally acquired immunity, would greatly facilitate this aim.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the goal of blocking transmission.

claim: Parasites that arrest during the liver stage can provide immunity against challenge infection.
source: Parasites that arrest during the liver stage, either because of irradiation (Nussenzweig et al., 1967) or targeted gene deletion (Mueller et al., 2005), can provide immunity against challenge infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on attenuated sporozoite vaccines.

claim: Immunization of human volunteers with irradiated sporozoites can induce sterile protection in experimental settings.
source: Indeed, immunization of human volunteers with irradiated sporozoites can induce sterile protection in experimental settings (Clyde et al., 1973; Seder et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical trials of irradiated sporozoite vaccines.

claim: A pre-erythrocytic vaccine that is only partially effective will provide no protection against severe malaria in the absence of acquired immunity to the blood-stage parasite.
source: However, in the absence of acquired immunity to the blood-stage parasite a pre-erythrocytic vaccine that is only partially effective, and therefore permits breakthrough erythrocytic infections, will provide no protection against severe malaria (Bejon et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on vaccine efficacy.

claim: The inclusion of a blood-stage component together with an effective pre-erythrocytic vaccine is preferred to provide a multi-stage malaria vaccine.
source: The inclusion of a blood-stage component together with an effective pre-erythrocytic vaccine is therefore preferred to provide a multi-stage malaria vaccine that minimizes both transmission and disease (Ellis et al., 2010; Goodman and Draper, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on multi-stage vaccine strategies.

claim: CPS immunization ensures exposure to pre-erythrocytic and blood-stage parasites.
source: A recently described experimental malaria immunization protocol using chemoprophylaxis and sporozoites (CPS) (Roestenberg et al., 2009) ensures exposure to pre-erythrocytic and blood-stage parasites, and hence has the unique potential to induce protection against all Plasmodium life cycle stages in the vertebrate host.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the original CPS protocol and logical inference about parasite exposure.

claim: Three immunizations with bites of 10–15 Plasmodium falciparum-infected mosquitoes under chloroquine chemoprophylaxis are sufficient to elicit sterile protection against homologous challenge in human volunteers.
source: Three immunizations with bites of 10–15 Plasmodium falciparum-infected mosquitoes under chloroquine chemoprophylaxis are sufficient to elicit sterile protection against homologous challenge in human volunteers (Roestenberg et al., 2009; Bijker et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human clinical trials of CPS immunization.

claim: In human CPS immunization trials, immunity exclusively targets pre-erythrocytic parasite life cycle stages.
source: Although it is not possible to measure liver parasite burden in human volunteers directly, it appears that immunity exclusively targets pre-erythrocytic parasite life cycle stages, as there is no protection against direct blood challenge (Bijker et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to clinical trial data showing no protection against blood-stage challenge.

claim: CPS immunization is substantially more effective than immunization with irradiated sporozoites.
source: CPS immunization is thus substantially more effective than immunization with irradiated sporozoites, which requires 1000 mosquito bites (Clyde et al., 1973) or five intravenous (iv) injections of more than 100,000 sporozoites for sterile protection (Seder et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations comparing the dose requirements of different immunization strategies.

claim: Transient blood-stage parasitemia before abrogation by chloroquine may contribute to immunity following CPS immunization.
source: We therefore hypothesize that transient blood-stage parasitemia, before abrogation by chloroquine, may contribute to immunity following CPS immunization.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis based on the observed efficacy of CPS.

claim: P. chabaudi establishes a chronic, non-lethal blood-stage infection.
source: P. chabaudi establishes a chronic, non-lethal blood-stage infection, which has been used extensively to characterize the immune response to blood-stage parasites in vivo (Stephens et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on P. chabaudi infection characteristics.

claim: A recently optimized protocol for P. chabaudi mosquito transmission allows study of pre-erythrocytic stages of this rodent parasite.
source: A recently optimized protocol for P. chabaudi mosquito transmission (Spence et al., 2012) allows us now to also study pre-erythrocytic stages of this rodent parasite.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published protocol.

claim: Many genetically distinct P. chabaudi isolates displaying a variety of virulence phenotypes are available.
source: Heterologous protection can readily be assessed since many genetically distinct P. chabaudi isolates displaying a variety of virulence phenotypes are available (Mackinnon and Read, 1999; Otto et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on P. chabaudi genetic diversity.

claim: C57BL/6 mice were immunized three times with bites of P. chabaudi-infected mosquitoes under oral chloroquine chemoprophylaxis similar to human clinical trials.
source: We immunized C57BL/6 mice three times with bites of P. chabaudi-infected mosquitoes under oral chloroquine chemoprophylaxis similar to human clinical trials (Roestenberg et al., 2009; Bijker et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: This approach is unique amongst all published animal models of CPS immunization.
source: This approach is unique amongst all published animal models of CPS immunization (Beaudoin et al., 1977; Golenser et al., 1977; Orjih et al., 1982; Belnoue et al., 2004; Friesen and Matuschewski, 2011; Inoue et al., 2012; Nganou-Makamdop et al., 2012b; Doll et al., 2014; Lewis et al., 2014; Peng et al., 2014), which have (without exception) used iv injection of high numbers of Plasmodium berghei or Plasmodium yoelii sporozoites for immunization.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous animal models and comparison of methods.

claim: Previous animal models of CPS immunization have used iv injection of high numbers of Plasmodium berghei or Plasmodium yoelii sporozoites for immunization.
source: This approach is unique amongst all published animal models of CPS immunization (Beaudoin et al., 1977; Golenser et al., 1977; Orjih et al., 1982; Belnoue et al., 2004; Friesen and Matuschewski, 2011; Inoue et al., 2012; Nganou-Makamdop et al., 2012b; Doll et al., 2014; Lewis et al., 2014; Peng et al., 2014), which have (without exception) used iv injection of high numbers of Plasmodium berghei or Plasmodium yoelii sporozoites for immunization.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous animal models.

claim: The challenge was performed 100 days after the final immunization to test the generation and maintenance of long-term immunological memory.
source: Furthermore, rather than evaluating effector mechanisms by challenging shortly after immunization (Beaudoin et al., 1977; Belnoue et al., 2004; Friesen and Matuschewski, 2011), we performed the challenge 100 days after the final immunization to test the generation and maintenance of long-term immunological memory.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design rationale.

claim: Immunization by bite elicits blood-stage immunity that is effective against the immunizing strain and also a more virulent, genetically distinct P. chabaudi.
source: Instead, immunization by bite elicits blood-stage immunity that is effective against the immunizing strain and also a more virulent, genetically distinct P. chabaudi.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing heterologous protection.

claim: Extended exposure to blood-stage parasitemia elicits robust pre-erythrocytic immunity, comparable to protection afforded by high dose sporozoite immunization.
source: Moreover, extended exposure to blood-stage parasitemia elicits robust pre-erythrocytic immunity, comparable to protection afforded by high dose sporozoite immunization.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced liver parasite burden after extended blood-stage infection.

claim: Exposure to blood-stage parasites elicits heterologous blood-stage immunity and can contribute to the pre-erythrocytic efficacy of this immunization regimen.
source: Exposure to blood-stage parasites thus elicits heterologous blood-stage immunity and can contribute to the pre-erythrocytic efficacy of this immunization regimen.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and logical inference from the results.

claim: After the first immunization, approximately 50,000 parasites per ml whole blood were detected within the first erythrocytic cycle.
source: After the first immunization, approximately 50,000 parasites per ml whole blood were detected within the first erythrocytic cycle (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT PCR data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The amount of blood-stage parasites within the first erythrocytic cycle varied extensively (median 47,596, range 67–222,699).
source: The amount of blood-stage parasites within the first erythrocytic cycle varied extensively (median 47,596, range 67–222,699), reflecting the stochastic inoculation of sporozoites during mosquito bite (Beier et al., 1991; Ponnudurai et al., 1991; Medica and Sinnis, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations explaining the biological basis for variation.

claim: Chloroquine reduced parasitemia by 86–96% every 24 hr.
source: Thereafter, chloroquine reduced parasitemia by 86–96% every 24 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT PCR measurements.

claim: After the fourth cycle, the majority of erythrocytic parasites were cleared.
source: After the fourth cycle, the majority of erythrocytic parasites were cleared.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Blood-stage parasites were detected in all but one mouse after each immunization.
source: However, although blood-stage parasites were detected in all but one mouse, parasitemia in the first erythrocytic cycle was reduced by 5- and 13-fold after the second and third immunizations, respectively, when compared to infection controls (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Parasitemia in the first erythrocytic cycle was reduced by 5- and 13-fold after the second and third immunizations, respectively, when compared to infection controls.
source: However, although blood-stage parasites were detected in all but one mouse, parasitemia in the first erythrocytic cycle was reduced by 5- and 13-fold after the second and third immunizations, respectively, when compared to infection controls (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: One CPS immunization is sufficient to reduce blood-stage parasite burden within the first erythrocytic cycle.
source: Consequently, one CPS immunization is sufficient to reduce blood-stage parasite burden within the first erythrocytic cycle, which indicates either pre-erythrocytic or blood-stage immunity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed reduction in parasitemia after the second immunization.

claim: There was no difference in the liver parasite burden between mice given three CPS immunizations with P. chabaudi AS-infected mosquito bites and infection controls.
source: Surprisingly, there was no difference in the liver parasite burden between mice given three CPS immunizations with P. chabaudi AS-infected mosquito bites and infection controls (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Immunization by mosquito bite under chloroquine cover according to this protocol failed to elicit pre-erythrocytic immunity.
source: Therefore, immunization by mosquito bite under chloroquine cover according to this protocol failed to elicit pre-erythrocytic immunity.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data showing no reduction in liver parasite burden.

claim: This is in contrast to results from other animal models of CPS immunization where pre-erythrocytic immunity is induced after high numbers of sporozoites are injected iv.
source: This is in contrast to results from other animal models of CPS immunization where pre-erythrocytic immunity is induced after high numbers of sporozoites are injected iv (Belnoue et al., 2004; Friesen and Matuschewski, 2011; Inoue et al., 2012; Nganou-Makamdop et al., 2012b; Lewis et al., 2014; Peng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mosquitoes infected with P. chabaudi CB harbor an increased number of sporozoites in their salivary glands compared to P. chabaudi AS.
source: To test if pre-erythrocytic immunity can be induced after CPS immunization with large numbers of sporozoites, we used P. chabaudi CB, since mosquitoes infected with this parasite strain harbor an increased number of sporozoites in their salivary glands compared to P. chabaudi AS (Spence et al., 2012), making these experiments technically feasible.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Mice immunized iv three times with 10,000 P. chabaudi CB sporozoites under chloroquine cover showed reduced liver parasite burden (up to 90%) after mosquito bite challenge.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Belnoue et al., 2004; Friesen and Matuschewski, 2011; Inoue et al., 2012; Nganou-Makamdop et al., 2012b; Lewis et al., 2014; Peng et al., 2014), mice immunized iv three times with 10,000 P. chabaudi CB sporozoites under chloroquine cover did show reduced liver parasite burden (up to 90%) after mosquito bite challenge, compared to infection controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B and citations to previous studies.

claim: Mice immunized iv three times with a low dose of 100 P. chabaudi CB sporozoites do not acquire pre-erythrocytic immunity.
source: Conversely, mice immunized iv three times with a low dose of 100 P. chabaudi CB sporozoites (representative of the estimated number of P. chabaudi sporozoites that initiate infection via mosquito bite, Spence et al., 2012) do not acquire pre-erythrocytic immunity (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: CPS immunization with 10,000 live sporozoites was more effective at inducing pre-erythrocytic immunity than immunization with 10,000 irradiated P. chabaudi CB sporozoites.
source: It also appears that CPS immunization with 10,000 live sporozoites was more effective at inducing pre-erythrocytic immunity than immunization with 10,000 irradiated P. chabaudi CB sporozoites, which arrest during hepatic development (Suhrbier et al., 1990) and do not establish a blood-stage infection (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B and citation to literature on irradiated sporozoites.

claim: Complete liver-stage maturation and the increased blood-stage parasitemia that accompanies immunization with 10,000 sporozoites could contribute to pre-erythrocytic protection.
source: This suggests that complete liver-stage maturation and the increased blood-stage parasitemia that accompanies immunization with 10,000 sporozoites (as compared to 100 sporozoites or mosquito bite) could contribute to pre-erythrocytic protection.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Mice that were CPS immunized with P. chabaudi AS had similar numbers of parasitized erythrocytes as compared to mock immunized controls within the first five erythrocytic cycles following mosquito bite challenge.
source: Mice that were CPS immunized with P. chabaudi AS had similar numbers of parasitized erythrocytes as compared to mock immunized controls within the first five erythrocytic cycles following mosquito bite challenge (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: From erythrocytic cycle 6 parasitemia was significantly reduced and blood-stage parasites were cleared more rapidly in immunized mice.
source: However, from erythrocytic cycle 6 parasitemia was significantly reduced and blood-stage parasites were cleared more rapidly in immunized mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: CPS immunization resulted in a 6-fold reduction of total area under the curve following homologous mosquito bite challenge.
source: This was reflected in a 6-fold reduction of total area under the curve (AUC) (right inset, Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Blood-stage parasitemia was significantly reduced following direct blood challenge with recently mosquito transmitted parasites.
source: Similar to the results of mosquito bite challenge, blood-stage parasitemia was significantly reduced (Figure 4B), but the infection was still chronic in some mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blood-stage protection was abrogated when CPS immunized mice were challenged with serially blood passaged (SBP) P. chabaudi.
source: However, blood-stage protection was abrogated when CPS immunized mice were challenged with serially blood passaged (SBP) P. chabaudi; blood-stage parasites with increased virulence following multiple passages through naive mice (Spence et al., 2013, Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C and citation to literature on SBP parasites.

claim: CPS immunization reduced blood-stage parasite burden only between erythrocytic cycle 6 and 8 when challenged with SBP parasites.
source: In this case, CPS immunization reduced blood-stage parasite burden only between erythrocytic cycle 6 and 8, as compared to mock immunized controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: CPS immunization resulted in only a 1.2-fold reduction in total AUC when challenged with SBP parasites.
source: This was reflected in only a 1.2-fold reduction in total AUC (right inset, Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: CPS immunization by mosquito bite elicits homologous blood-stage immunity, which is most effective in the context of mosquito transmission.
source: Therefore, CPS immunization by mosquito bite elicits homologous blood-stage immunity, which is most effective in the context of mosquito transmission.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential protection observed against mosquito transmitted vs. SBP parasites.

claim: Mice that were CPS immunized with P. chabaudi AS-infected mosquito bites had reduced peak parasitemia when compared to mock immunized mice after homologous and heterologous mosquito bite challenge.
source: Mice that were CPS immunized with P. chabaudi AS-infected mosquito bites had reduced peak parasitemia, and blood-stage parasites were cleared faster, when compared to mock immunized mice after homologous (P. chabaudi AS) and heterologous (P. chabaudi CB) mosquito bite challenge (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Blood-stage parasites were cleared faster in CPS immunized mice when compared to mock immunized mice after homologous and heterologous mosquito bite challenge.
source: Mice that were CPS immunized with P. chabaudi AS-infected mosquito bites had reduced peak parasitemia, and blood-stage parasites were cleared faster, when compared to mock immunized mice after homologous (P. chabaudi AS) and heterologous (P. chabaudi CB) mosquito bite challenge (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Homologous blood-stage immunity is more effective than heterologous immunity.
source: A direct comparison between P. chabaudi AS and CB challenge revealed nonetheless that homologous blood-stage immunity is more effective than heterologous immunity.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of experimental data from homologous and heterologous challenges.

claim: CPS immunization reduced total AUC by 25-fold following homologous challenge.
source: In this experiment, CPS immunization reduced total AUC by 25-fold following homologous challenge, as compared to 6-fold following heterologous challenge (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: CPS immunization reduced total AUC by 6-fold following heterologous challenge.
source: In this experiment, CPS immunization reduced total AUC by 25-fold following homologous challenge, as compared to 6-fold following heterologous challenge (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: CPS immunization elicits blood-stage protection against a robust heterologous challenge with the genetically distinct, and more virulent, CB strain of P. chabaudi.
source: Nevertheless, CPS immunization elicits blood-stage protection against a robust heterologous challenge with the genetically distinct, and more virulent, CB strain of P. chabaudi.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced parasitemia after heterologous challenge.

claim: Immunization with serially blood passaged P. yoelii parasites with prophylactic chloroquine treatment can elicit pre-erythrocytic immunity.
source: It was shown that immunization with serially blood passaged P. yoelii parasites with prophylactic chloroquine treatment can elicit pre-erythrocytic immunity (Belnoue et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Mice infected with P. chabaudi AS by mosquito bite or ip injection of recently mosquito transmitted blood-stage parasites experienced a low-grade chronic, recrudescing blood-stage infection for up to 90 days.
source: We infected mice with P. chabaudi AS by mosquito bite or intraperitoneal (ip) injection of recently mosquito transmitted blood-stage parasites. The two groups of mice were not drug-treated, and therefore experienced a low-grade chronic, recrudescing blood-stage infection for up to 90 days (Spence et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental design and citation to literature on P. chabaudi infection dynamics.

claim: Both groups of mice demonstrated reduced liver parasite burden (up to 85%) after mosquito bite challenge, compared to infection controls.
source: After mosquito bite challenge, both groups of mice demonstrated reduced liver parasite burden (up to 85%), compared to infection controls (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Cross-stage immunity is a powerful mechanism for protection against pre-erythrocytic parasites.
source: Cross-stage immunity is therefore a powerful mechanism for protection against pre-erythrocytic parasites, which may be absent during CPS immunization with small sporozoite numbers as the blood-stage infection is curtailed by the use of chloroquine.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing pre-erythrocytic protection after blood-stage infection.

claim: Cross-stage immunity may be absent during CPS immunization with small sporozoite numbers as the blood-stage infection is curtailed by the use of chloroquine.
source: Cross-stage immunity is therefore a powerful mechanism for protection against pre-erythrocytic parasites, which may be absent during CPS immunization with small sporozoite numbers as the blood-stage infection is curtailed by the use of chloroquine.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why CPS immunization by bite did not induce pre-erythrocytic immunity.

claim: Timing, route of infection, and antigen dose play major roles in determining the initial priming of the antimalarial immune response.
source: Timing, route of infection, and antigen dose play major roles in determining the initial priming of the antimalarial immune response (Legorreta-Herrera et al., 2004; Elliott et al., 2005; Belnoue et al., 2008; Guilbride et al., 2012; Nganou-Makamdop et al., 2012a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on immune priming.

claim: Pre-erythrocytic immunity appears to depend on the number of immunizing sporozoites.
source: Pre-erythrocytic immunity appears to depend on the number of immunizing sporozoites.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing dose-dependent pre-erythrocytic immunity.

claim: Anopheles stephensi mosquitoes experimentally infected with P. falciparum 3D7 or NF54 harbor 50–200 times more sporozoites in their salivary glands compared to P. chabaudi AS.
source: Anopheles stephensi mosquitoes experimentally infected with P. falciparum 3D7 or NF54 habor 50–200 times more sporozoites in their salivary glands (Bijker et al., 2013) compared to P. chabaudi AS (Spence et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies measuring sporozoite loads.

claim: Only few sporozoites are injected into the skin during mosquito bite and this number is independent of salivary gland sporozoites load.
source: However, only few sporozoites are injected into the skin during mosquito bite and this number is independent of salivary gland sporozoites load (Beier et al., 1991; Ponnudurai et al., 1991; Medica and Sinnis, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on sporozoite inoculation.

claim: The number of sporozoites establishing a liver-stage infection can be influenced by inherent sporozoite infectivity.
source: Since the number of sporozoites establishing a liver-stage infection can further be influenced by inherent sporozoite infectivity (Khan and Vanderberg, 1991), our best estimate of immunizing sporozoite dose is the number of infected erythrocytes observed directly after egress from the liver.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on sporozoite infectivity.

claim: Approximately 10,000 merozoites are released from one infected liver cell.
source: Assuming that 10,000 merozoites are released from one infected liver cell (White et al., 2014), we estimate approximately 400 infected hepatocytes (95% CI 137–1250) in human volunteers (Bijker et al., 2013) compared to 5 in P. chabaudi AS immunized mice (95% CI 1–31).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on merozoite release.

claim: Approximately 400 infected hepatocytes (95% CI 137–1250) are present in human CPS volunteers.
source: Assuming that 10,000 merozoites are released from one infected liver cell (White et al., 2014), we estimate approximately 400 infected hepatocytes (95% CI 137–1250) in human volunteers (Bijker et al., 2013) compared to 5 in P. chabaudi AS immunized mice (95% CI 1–31).
evidence: This is a calculation based on data from cited studies.

claim: Approximately 5 infected hepatocytes (95% CI 1–31) are present in P. chabaudi AS immunized mice.
source: Assuming that 10,000 merozoites are released from one infected liver cell (White et al., 2014), we estimate approximately 400 infected hepatocytes (95% CI 137–1250) in human volunteers (Bijker et al., 2013) compared to 5 in P. chabaudi AS immunized mice (95% CI 1–31).
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data from this study.

claim: The number of infected hepatocytes after CPS immunization by mosquito bite in the P. chabaudi mouse model is approximately 100-fold lower than in CPS immunized humans.
source: Therefore, the number of infected hepatocytes after CPS immunization by mosquito bite in the P. chabaudi mouse model is approximately 100-fold lower than in CPS immunized humans.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of calculated values.

claim: Differences in infected hepatocyte numbers by a factor of 100 can be significant for the development of pre-erythrocytic immunity.
source: We show that this differences in infected hepatocyte numbers by a factor of 100 can be significant for the development of pre-erythrocytic immunity: three immunizations with 10,000 P. chabaudi sporozoites iv induce long-lasting protection against mosquito bite challenge, while three immunizations with 100 P. chabaudi sporozoites fail to do so.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different sporozoite doses.

claim: Sterile pre-erythrocytic immunity is observed after immunization with high sporozoite doses (typically 10,000–50,000 sporozoites per immunization) in rodent malaria studies.
source: This is in general agreement with other rodent malaria studies using P. berghei (Beaudoin et al., 1977; Golenser et al., 1977; Orjih et al., 1982; Friesen and Matuschewski, 2011; Nganou-Makamdop et al., 2012b; Lewis et al., 2014) or P. yoelii (Belnoue et al., 2004; Inoue et al., 2012; Doll et al., 2014; Peng et al., 2014), in which sterile pre-erythrocytic immunity is observed after immunization with high sporozoite doses (typically 10,000–50,000 sporozoites per immunization), while a reduction in sporozoite dose or the number of immunizations leads to breakthrough blood-stage infections upon challenge (Belnoue et al., 2004; Inoue et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple rodent malaria studies.

claim: A reduction in sporozoite dose or the number of immunizations leads to breakthrough blood-stage infections upon challenge.
source: This is in general agreement with other rodent malaria studies using P. berghei (Beaudoin et al., 1977; Golenser et al., 1977; Orjih et al., 1982; Friesen and Matuschewski, 2011; Nganou-Makamdop et al., 2012b; Lewis et al., 2014) or P. yoelii (Belnoue et al., 2004; Inoue et al., 2012; Doll et al., 2014; Peng et al., 2014), in which sterile pre-erythrocytic immunity is observed after immunization with high sporozoite doses (typically 10,000–50,000 sporozoites per immunization), while a reduction in sporozoite dose or the number of immunizations leads to breakthrough blood-stage infections upon challenge (Belnoue et al., 2004; Inoue et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing dose-dependent protection.

claim: Reduction of the number of P. falciparum-infected mosquitoes reduces the frequency of sterilely protected volunteers.
source: Reduction of the number of P. falciparum-infected mosquitoes also reduces the frequency of sterilely protected volunteers (Bijker et al., 2014), indicating that the number of sporozoites establishing a liver-stage infection fails to surpass the protective threshold to elicit sterile pre-erythrocytic immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a clinical trial.

claim: In malaria-endemic areas pre-erythrocytic immunity is thought to be absent.
source: This may also explain why in malaria-endemic areas pre-erythrocytic immunity is thought to be absent (Tran et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on naturally acquired immunity.

claim: CPS immunization with high numbers of sporozoites may broaden the immune repertoire by including protective responses against subdominant antigens.
source: In addition to maximizing specific responses against immunodominant antigens, CPS immunization with high numbers of sporozoites may broaden the immune repertoire by including protective responses against subdominant antigens, which could enhance heterologous pre-erythrocytic protection (Trieu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to literature on immune responses.

claim: P. falciparum liver-stage development is longer (egress 6.8 days after mosquito bite) compared to P. chabaudi (egress after 52 hr).
source: This may further be enhanced by the longer liver-stage development of P. falciparum (egress 6.8 days after mosquito bite, Roestenberg et al., 2012) compared to P. chabaudi (egress after 52 hr, Stephens et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on liver-stage development timing.

claim: Longer liver stage development may positively influence the generation of pre-erythrocytic immunity by allowing time for protective immune responses to develop.
source: Longer liver stage development may positively influence the generation of pre-erythrocytic immunity by allowing time for protective immune responses to develop.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how liver-stage duration might affect immunity.

claim: Repeated exposure to blood-stage parasites induces blood-stage immunity in rodent models.
source: It is well known that repeated exposure to blood-stage parasites, for example, in rodent models (Jarra and Brown, 1985; Legorreta-Herrera et al., 2004; Elliott et al., 2005), in humans exposed to ultra-low doses of parasitized erythrocytes while receiving drug treatment (Pombo et al., 2002), during malaria-therapy of neurosyphilis patients (Collins and Jeffery, 1999), and in people living in malaria-endemic areas (Bull et al., 1998), induces blood-stage immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on blood-stage immunity.

claim: Repeated exposure to blood-stage parasites induces blood-stage immunity in humans exposed to ultra-low doses of parasitized erythrocytes while receiving drug treatment.
source: It is well known that repeated exposure to blood-stage parasites, for example, in rodent models (Jarra and Brown, 1985; Legorreta-Herrera et al., 2004; Elliott et al., 2005), in humans exposed to ultra-low doses of parasitized erythrocytes while receiving drug treatment (Pombo et al., 2002), during malaria-therapy of neurosyphilis patients (Collins and Jeffery, 1999), and in people living in malaria-endemic areas (Bull et al., 1998), induces blood-stage immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a human study.

claim: Repeated exposure to blood-stage parasites induces blood-stage immunity during malaria-therapy of neurosyphilis patients.
source: It is well known that repeated exposure to blood-stage parasites, for example, in rodent models (Jarra and Brown, 1985; Legorreta-Herrera et al., 2004; Elliott et al., 2005), in humans exposed to ultra-low doses of parasitized erythrocytes while receiving drug treatment (Pombo et al., 2002), during malaria-therapy of neurosyphilis patients (Collins and Jeffery, 1999), and in people living in malaria-endemic areas (Bull et al., 1998), induces blood-stage immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to historical malaria therapy studies.

claim: Repeated exposure to blood-stage parasites induces blood-stage immunity in people living in malaria-endemic areas.
source: It is well known that repeated exposure to blood-stage parasites, for example, in rodent models (Jarra and Brown, 1985; Legorreta-Herrera et al., 2004; Elliott et al., 2005), in humans exposed to ultra-low doses of parasitized erythrocytes while receiving drug treatment (Pombo et al., 2002), during malaria-therapy of neurosyphilis patients (Collins and Jeffery, 1999), and in people living in malaria-endemic areas (Bull et al., 1998), induces blood-stage immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to studies on naturally acquired immunity.

claim: During CPS immunization repeated transient blood-stage infection (less than 0.01% parasitemia for 48–72 hr) elicits long-lasting blood-stage immunity.
source: Our results also clearly show that during CPS immunization repeated transient blood-stage infection (less than 0.01% parasitemia for 48–72 hr) elicits long-lasting blood-stage immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from this study.

claim: Protection against challenge infection was only apparent after multiple erythrocytic replication cycles and patent blood-stage parasite densities.
source: Protection against challenge infection was only apparent after multiple erythrocytic replication cycles and patent blood-stage parasite densities, which could indicate that blood-stage protection was not observed in CPS immunized human volunteers after direct blood-challenge because drug treatment is required at low parasite densities as soon as patency is reached (typically between the third and fourth erythrocytic cycle, Bijker et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to human trial protocols.

claim: Blood-stage parasites are recognized in human CPS volunteers, as demonstrated by an earlier increase of IFNγ and MIG concentrations compared to infection controls after direct blood challenge.
source: Blood-stage parasites are however recognized in human volunteers, which was demonstrated by an earlier increase of IFNγ and monokines induced by IFNγ (MIG) concentrations in CPS immunized volunteers compared to infection controls after direct blood challenge (Bijker et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to immunological data from human trials.

claim: Recrudescent parasitemia could be observed in the chronic phase of infection after challenge in CPS immunized mice, suggesting a parasite variant escapes the protective immune response.
source: Despite the reduced peak parasitemia and faster clearance of blood-stage parasites during the acute phase of infection in CPS immunized mice, recrudescent parasitemia could still be observed in the chronic phase of infection after challenge, suggesting a parasite variant escapes the protective immune response (McLean et al., 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to literature on antigenic variation.

claim: There are very few reports on protective efficacy of CPS immunization against direct blood-challenge.
source: There are very few reports on protective efficacy of CPS immunization (or indeed any sporozoite-based vaccine) against direct blood-challenge (Belnoue et al., 2004; Inoue et al., 2012; Peng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the limited literature on this topic.

claim: Sustained, subpatent blood-stage infection after treatment with chloroquine can induce partial blood-stage protection.
source: Doll et al. (2014) reported that sustained, subpatent blood-stage infection after treatment with a commonly used dose of chloroquine can induce partial blood-stage protection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Low-grade transient blood-stage parasitemia provides protection against homologous and heterologous blood-stage challenge.
source: Low-grade transient blood-stage parasitemia, achieved by attenuation of blood-stage parasites using an antimalarial drug (Pombo et al., 2002; Elliott et al., 2005), a DNA alkylating agent (Good et al., 2013) or genetic tools (Ting et al., 2008; Aly et al., 2010) similarly provides protection against homologous and heterologous blood-stage challenge.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on attenuated blood-stage vaccines.

claim: CPS-induced blood-stage immunity is effective against heterologous mosquito bite challenge with a more virulent and genetically distinct strain of P. chabaudi.
source: We could show that CPS-induced blood-stage immunity is effective against heterologous mosquito bite challenge with a more virulent and genetically distinct strain of P. chabaudi (Mackinnon and Read, 1999; Lamb and Langhorne, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations characterizing the parasite strains.

claim: Heterologous protection after CPS immunization is less effective than homologous immunity.
source: In agreement with the observed cross-species protection after CPS immunization with mefloquine (Inoue et al., 2012), and one study using chemically attenuated sporozoites for immunization (Purcell et al., 2008), heterologous protection is less effective than homologous immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: CPS immunization can elicit long-lived protection against both homologous and heterologous blood-stage parasites.
source: Nevertheless, CPS immunization can elicit long-lived protection against both homologous and heterologous blood-stage parasites, which will be important to minimize disease severity in the case of breakthrough blood-stage infections.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from this study.

claim: Heterologous blood-stage protection is essential for the development of an effective multi-stage malaria vaccine.
source: Nevertheless, CPS immunization can elicit long-lived protection against both homologous and heterologous blood-stage parasites, which will be important to minimize disease severity in the case of breakthrough blood-stage infections. This is essential for the development of an effective multi-stage malaria vaccine (Ellis et al., 2010; Bejon et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on inference and citations to literature on vaccine development.

claim: Blood-stage parasites immediately after mosquito transmission express antigens not present on serially blood passaged parasites.
source: This suggests that blood-stage parasites immediately after mosquito transmission express antigens not present on serially blood passaged parasites and that these antigens may be the target of protective immunity following CPS immunization.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differential protection observed.

claim: Serially blood passaged parasites can escape from CPS-induced blood-stage immunity.
source: Serially blood passaged parasites can hence escape from CPS-induced blood-stage immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing loss of protection against SBP parasites.

claim: Transcription of more than half of all cir genes is increased in blood-stage parasites after mosquito transmission compared with their transcription after serial blood passage.
source: Transcription of more than half of all cir genes is increased in blood-stage parasites after mosquito transmission compared with their transcription after serial blood passage.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on cir gene expression.

claim: Diversification of cir transcription is associated with a more effective host immune response, which in turn attenuates parasite virulence.
source: This diversification of cir transcription is associated with a more effective host immune response, which in turn attenuates parasite virulence (Spence et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: P. berghei pir genes are transcribed during the liver stages.
source: The cir genes could also be candidate targets for cross-stage immunity, as P. berghei pir genes are also transcribed during the liver stages (personal communication BM Franke-Fayard and CJ Janse, Leiden University Medical Center, The Netherlands).
evidence: This claim is supported by personal communication cited in the manuscript.

claim: The absence of blood-stage protection in previous CPS models may have been due to challenge with serially blood passaged rather than recently mosquito transmitted blood-stage parasites.
source: Furthermore, the absence of blood-stage protection in previous CPS models may have been due to challenge with serially blood passaged rather then recently mosquito transmitted blood-stage parasites.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of previous negative results.

claim: It is essential to evaluate blood-stage immunity in the context of mosquito transmission.
source: It is therefore always essential to evaluate blood-stage immunity in the context of mosquito transmission.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Shared antigenic targets between liver- and blood-stage parasites have been described.
source: As shared antigenic targets between liver- and blood-stage parasites have been described (Tarun et al., 2008), the exciting possibility of cross-stage protection has been considered but only rarely assessed.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on shared antigens.

claim: Genetically modified fabb/f- sporozoites that arrest late in liver-stage development protect against iv challenge with 100 blood-stage parasites.
source: Genetically modified fabb/f- sporozoites that arrest late in liver-stage development protect against iv challenge with 100 blood-stage parasites (Butler et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: A blood-stage infection with serially blood passaged P. yoelii, drug-treated with chloroquine after 4–5 days, reduces liver parasite load upon iv challenge with 35,000 sporozoites.
source: On the other hand, a blood-stage infection with serially blood passaged P. yoelii, drug-treated with chloroquine after 4–5 days, reduces liver parasite load upon iv challenge with 35,000 sporozoites (Belnoue et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Repeated transient blood-stage infection during immunization likely elicits the observed blood-stage protection.
source: In our model of CPS immunization by mosquito bite, it is likely that repeated transient blood-stage infection during immunization elicits the observed blood-stage protection, although we cannot yet exclude that responses acquired against pre-erythrocytic antigens, which are shared with blood-stage parasites (Tarun et al., 2008), contribute as well.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results with acknowledgment of alternative explanations.

claim: Extended exposure to blood-stage parasites is an effective stimulator of pre-erythrocytic immunity.
source: Nevertheless, we demonstrate unequivocally that extended exposure to blood-stage parasites is an effective stimulator of pre-erythrocytic immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing pre-erythrocytic protection after blood-stage infection.

claim: Exposure to blood-stage parasites during CPS immunization may significantly contribute to the observed pre-erythrocytic protection in human volunteers.
source: Exposure to blood-stage parasites during CPS immunization may thus significantly contribute to the observed pre-erythrocytic protection in human volunteers (Roestenberg et al., 2009; Bijker et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the mouse data to human trials.

claim: Cross-stage immunity could be responsible for the unprecedented efficacy of CPS immunization compared to immunization with irradiated sporozoites.
source: Indeed, cross-stage immunity could be responsible for the unprecedented efficacy of CPS immunization compared to immunization with irradiated sporozoites (Clyde et al., 1973; Seder et al., 2013), which arrest early during liver-stage development and never establish a blood-stage infection.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: Irradiated sporozoites arrest early during liver-stage development and never establish a blood-stage infection.
source: Indeed, cross-stage immunity could be responsible for the unprecedented efficacy of CPS immunization compared to immunization with irradiated sporozoites (Clyde et al., 1973; Seder et al., 2013), which arrest early during liver-stage development and never establish a blood-stage infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and citations about irradiated sporozoites.

claim: The incorporation of chemically or genetically attenuated blood-stage parasites should be considered to further enhance the generation and maintenance of both pre-erythrocytic and blood-stage immunity.
source: While extending exposure to replicating blood-stage parasites by delayed drug administration is not possible in humans, the incorporation of chemically (Good et al., 2013) or genetically (Ting et al., 2008; Aly et al., 2010) attenuated blood-stage parasites should be considered to further enhance the generation and maintenance of both pre-erythrocytic and blood-stage immunity.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings and citations to relevant technologies.

claim: CPS immunization is a powerful tool for the development of an effective multi-stage malaria vaccine.
source: This makes CPS immunization a powerful tool for the development of an effective multi-stage malaria vaccine.
evidence: This is a concluding statement based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: Mice were exposed to typically 9.15 (median, range 6.9–13.6) P. chabaudi-infected mosquito bites.
source: To quantify transient blood-stage exposure during chemoprophylaxis and sporozoite (CPS) immunization female C57BL/6 were immunized three times at 2-week intervals with P. chabaudi AS-infected mosquito bites (typically 9.15 [median, range 6.9–13.6] [Spence et al., 2012]).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental protocol with data from a cited study.

claim: P. chabaudi develops in the liver for 52 hr.
source: A small blood sample was taken 48 hr after each mosquito transmission (before merozoite egress from the liver, P. chabaudi develops in the liver for 52 hr [Stephens et al., 2012]; erythrocytic cycle 0), and then every 24 hr until erythrocytic replication cycle 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on P. chabaudi liver-stage development.

claim: P. chabaudi CB was used for high-dose sporozoite immunization experiments since mosquitoes infected with this parasite harbor an increased number of sporozoites in their salivary glands.
source: P. chabaudi CB was used since mosquitoes infected with this parasite harbor an increased number of sporozoites in their salivary glands (Spence et al., 2012), which made injections of high numbers of sporozoites technically feasible.
evidence: This claim explains the experimental design choice with citation to supporting data.

claim: All experiments were performed in accordance with UK Home Office regulations (PPL 80/2358) and approved by the ethical review panel at the MRC NIMR.
source: All experiments were performed in accordance with UK Home Office regulations (PPL 80/2358) and approved by the ethical review panel at the MRC NIMR.
evidence: This is a statement of regulatory compliance.

claim: P. chabaudi AS and CB were cloned at the University of Edinburgh and sent to the NIMR in 1978 and 1982, respectively.
source: Plasmodium chabaudi chabaudi (P. chabaudi) AS and CB were cloned at the University of Edinburgh and sent to the NIMR in 1978 and 1982, respectively.
evidence: This describes the provenance of the parasite strains used.

claim: P. chabaudi CB sporozoites were isolated from mosquito salivary glands 15 or 16 days post gametocyte feed.
source: Sporozoites were isolated from P. chabaudi-infected mosquito salivary glands 15 or 16 days post gametocyte feed.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: P. chabaudi CB infected A. stephensi were exposed to 16 Gray of Caesium-137 γ-irradiation to arrest parasite development in the early stages of liver development.
source: To arrest parasite development in the early stages of liver development P. chabaudi CB infected A. stephensi were exposed to 16 Gray (=16,000 rad) (Nganou-Makamdop et al., 2012b) of Caesium-137 γ-irradiation 15 or 16 days post gametocyte feed just prior to sporozoite dissection.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol with citation to the irradiation dose used.

claim: Mice were treated after each immunization with 100 mg/kg chloroquine diphosphate salt by gavage daily for 10 days.
source: Mice were treated after each immunization with 100 mg/kg chloroquine diphosphate salt (chloroquine, Sigma, Gillingham, UK) by gavage daily for 10 days, starting from the day of mosquito transmission.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Each erythrocytic cycle of P. chabaudi is approximately 24 hr long.
source: Since each erythrocytic cycle of P. chabaudi is approximately 24 hr long (Stephens et al., 2012) development of blood-stage parasitemia was monitored daily by microscopy of Giemsa-stained thin blood films, from erythrocytic cycle 3 to 14 and every other day thereafter.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on P. chabaudi biology.

claim: The limit of detection by thin blood film is 0.01% parasitemia.
source: The limit of detection was 0.01% parasitemia, which equals 1 parasitized red blood cell in 10,000 erythrocytes or 1,000,000 parasitized erythrocytes per ml of blood.
evidence: This describes the technical limitation of the detection method.

claim: Liver parasitemia was examined 42 hr after challenge by qRT PCR.
source: Liver parasitemia was examined 42 hr after challenge by qRT PCR.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: P. chabaudi displays a synchronous infection.
source: Since P. chabaudi displays a synchronous infection (Stephens et al., 2012) all blood-stage parasites analyzed were therefore at the late trophozoite stage of development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on P. chabaudi infection characteristics.
